title: Chapter 252: Not Human
html:
It was exactly midnight when the passenger returned to the car. He cradled the black package and hid his face beneath his hood. The red of his shirt seemed darker now. Uncle Zhang tried not to look in the mirror, but his gaze kept drifting toward it.

“Why does it feel as though someone else came back?” Uncle Zhang murmured, opening the emergency screen on his phone.

“Going back to Huai Hua Street?”

“Yes.”

“Do you live there? Mostly elderly people remain in Jiujiang’s old quarter. Someone your age would be unusual.”

“No. I don’t live there.” His tone was strange, every short reply heavy and dark.

“From your accent, I’d say you’re a Jiujiang local. The nights have been dangerous lately. You should go home rather than wander around.” Uncle Zhang dreaded returning to that cursed street and encountering another strange passenger. “Where do you live? Why don’t I take you home instead?”

“My home?” The passenger lowered his head farther, focusing on the black package in his lap, and said nothing more. Too uncomfortable to press him, Uncle Zhang turned the taxi back toward the city.

Once the car began moving, the atmosphere grew even more oppressive. Sharing the confined space with his passenger left Uncle Zhang struggling to breathe. He opened the windows, and the night breeze revived him slightly. Then he looked back.

No matter how the car jolted, the passenger’s upper body remained fixed. His wrinkled T-shirt suggested he had dressed in haste. Its collar hung open, exposing a faint ligature mark.

Was he assaulted inside the crematorium? Wait, those looks like marks left behind from a hanging!

Uncle Zhang grew even more nervous. He kept half his attention on the passenger, afraid something would happen the moment he looked away.

Uncle Zhang’s pupils trembled, and his heart raced. He feared the passenger might notice his scrutiny, but feared even more what the man might do. Pressing harder on the accelerator seemed the safest choice. Once they reached the crowded city, he should be safe.

Wind poured through the open windows while Uncle Zhang watched the rear seat. The passenger sat frozen, but one corner of the black cloth lifted from the object on his lap. The fabric slid aside, exposing the package beneath.

Blood surged to Uncle Zhang’s head, and his heart pounded. It was a funerary urn. The object the man had retrieved from the crematorium was an urn.

His arms started to shake, and his fingers curled inward like he was suffering from an involuntary spasm. A chill climbed his spine.

The passenger appeared not to notice the exposed urn. As the taxi sped along, the wind peeled away the rest of the cloth.

Uncle Zhang could now see clearly. The black cloth had concealed a black urn bearing a photograph. He eased off the accelerator and focused on the portrait. Though details remained indistinct, its chin and lips resembled those of his passenger.

He went to the crematorium to retrieve his own urn in the middle of the night?

Uncle Zhang dared not complete the thought. His entire body trembled. Keeping one hand on the wheel, he reached for his phone to call the police. But as his fingers touched it, habit drew his eyes to the mirror—and a pair of bloodshot eyes stared back.

The passenger had raised his head. His face matched the portrait on the urn, only much paler. Uncle Zhang’s skin crawled. Years of experience alone kept the car on the road.

The taxi continued toward the city, only minutes away, but Uncle Zhang’s situation worsened. The passenger fixed his gaze upon the rearview mirror, ensuring that every glance met those bloodshot eyes.

The breeze had blown the black cloth away, so the passenger sat in the back, completely unmoving, holding his own urn in his lap.

“What is he thinking?!”

No other vehicles shared the road. Panic burned in Uncle Zhang’s chest, and the route began to feel wrong—as though he were driving not toward the city but deeper into the countryside.

“What do I do?” He had contacted the police and sent an SOS to the drivers’ group, but no one was nearby. Each time he glanced at the mirror, the passenger’s eyes seemed closer.

He clutched the wheel as the temperature fell. Though pressed against the seat, he could no longer feel its cushioning.

The phone he had dropped beside him began vibrating. Someone was calling, but Uncle Zhang did not dare answer.

“Hey.” The passenger spoke without warning, making Uncle Zhang shiver.

Two seconds later, he said, “Y… Yes?”

“Someone is calling you.”

Uncle Zhang looked at his phone. The one-touch police screen had vanished, replaced by an incoming call from an unknown number. It ended quickly, as though the caller had realized something was wrong.

“Ignore it. Talking on the phone while driving is unsafe anyway.” Uncle Zhang laughed dryly.

Then he glanced at the phone again—a message had come in.

“Quickly stop your car! Run down the road as fast as you can! It’s not a human being sitting at the back of your car!”

The message remained on-screen for several seconds. Uncle Zhang saw it—and so did the passenger. “My friend is always joking.”

Uncle Zhang moved the phone beside the steering wheel. He was about to speak when he looked up and found the passenger’s face pressed against the security partition.

There was an inexplicable smile on the passenger’s face.

“There’s no reason to pretend. I’m sure you’ve already noticed.” The hood slipped down. The passenger’s neck slowly twisted, revealing another face growing from the back of his head.

“Technically, he is still human, but I’m not.” This sentence was said by the face on the back.

Uncle Zhang’s mind went blank. Acting on instinct, he stamped on the brake. The taxi skidded several meters before stopping, and he fled the car screaming.

The passenger climbed out as well. Turning his back on Uncle Zhang, he revealed an ugly smile on the face behind his head.

“There’s nowhere to run. This body has been targeted by a madman, so I need a new partner.”

With his back still turned toward Uncle Zhang, the passenger pursued him in reverse, moving like a puppet dragged by invisible strings.
